assessment:
This study addresses a significant technical challenge in planarian neurobiology by developing and applying an integrated imaging approach combining tissue expansion (C-MAP) with tiling light-sheet microscopy (TLSM) to achieve comprehensive 3D visualization of the planarian nervous system at nanoscale resolution. The authors successfully optimized the C-MAP protocol for planarians, achieving up to 4.5-fold linear expansion within 48 hours and imaging resolutions of 120-500 nm, which represents a substantial improvement in throughput and accessibility compared to conventional confocal approaches. The development of an automatic 3D cell segmentation pipeline enabled quantitative profiling of neurons and muscle fibers at single-cell resolution across an impressive dataset of over 400 planarians during homeostasis and 251 samples during regeneration.

The study makes several important contributions to understanding planarian neurobiology and regeneration. First, the comprehensive quantitative analysis of five neuron types (cholinergic, serotonergic, GABAergic, dopaminergic, octopaminergic) across different body sizes revealed that neurons comprise approximately 10% of total body cells in planarians smaller than 7 mm, but this proportion significantly decreases in larger animals. This threshold phenomenon, while speculative in its connection to fission, represents a novel observation that warrants further investigation. Second, the regeneration time-course analysis with daily sampling over 14 days provided enhanced resolution of the biphasic dynamics of neuron regeneration, validating and extending prior observations with substantially larger sample sizes. The differential regeneration kinetics between neuron types and between anatomical regions (brain vs. branches, dorsal-lateral vs. ventral-medial) suggest distinct regulatory mechanisms that merit further mechanistic investigation. Third, the high-resolution muscle fiber imaging revealed previously unappreciated structural details, including distinct anterior-posterior differences in muscle integration patterns and their correlation with body axis polarity, as demonstrated through β-catenin-1 RNAi experiments.

The study's most intriguing but also most speculative findings concern the proposed role of muscle fibers as scaffolds for neuron projection and guidance during regeneration. While the close spatial correlations between muscle fibers and neurons/glia are well-documented through extensive dual-labeling experiments, and the temporal correlation during regeneration is compelling, the directional relationship and functional significance remain to be established through perturbation experiments. The RNAi experiments with inr-1 and β-catenin-1 provide correlative evidence linking muscle structure to glial projections, but the authors appropriately acknowledge that distinguishing cell-autonomous from non-autonomous effects requires further investigation. The claim that muscle serves as a scaffold for neural guidance, while plausible, represents an interpretation that extends beyond the direct observations.

Several methodological considerations should be noted. The authors acknowledge that the 6G10 antibody preferentially labels circular and diagonal muscle fibers, which may limit the completeness of muscle fiber characterization. The segmentation pipeline, while validated through comparison with manual counting, may have limitations in resolving densely packed nerve tracts. The neuron pool comprising five markers does not include glutamatergic, glycinergic, and peptidergic neurons, which limits the interpretation of the non-linear neuron-to-cell ratio dynamics. Despite these limitations, the study represents a significant technical advance that enables systematic, quantitative analysis of planarian neuroanatomy and regeneration at unprecedented scale and resolution. The comprehensive dataset, rigorous quantification, and integration of homeostatic and regenerative analyses provide a valuable resource for the planarian research community and demonstrate the broader applicability of this imaging approach to other regenerative organisms.
